newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: CURLING-DESPERATE CURLERS BEG FUNDS FROM IOC.
newsitem.headline: CURLING-DESPERATE CURLERS BEG FUNDS FROM IOC.

text.p: The cash-strapped organisers of the world curling championships have been forced to beg $400,000 from the IOC to ensure the sport is able to make its Olympic debut in Nagano next year.
The World Curling Federation (WCF) will not officially become part of the Olympic family for another year but has successfully applied for a cash advance to ease its mounting financial problems.
Last year's world championships in Hamilton, Ontario, lost a reported $400,000 and the Berne organisers are bracing themselves for an even bigger loss this time.
Normally, Olympic funds are distributed to the different member sports by the IOC after each Olympic Games to help see them through the next four years.

The WCF has persuaded the IOC to hand over the money in advance but the cash infusion will do nothing to solve the former's other immediate problem -- a world championships fast turning into an embarrassment.
IOC president Juan Antonio Samaranch will attend the men's final on Sunday but is unlikely to be impressed by the crowd of around 3,000 which organisers are predicting.
The round-robin portion of the competition, stretched out over six days, attracted a total of just 13,201 spectators to the cavernous Allmend arena which has a daily capacity of over 16,000.
With no Swiss teams reaching Friday's semifinals, officials have expressed fears there will be little interest left for the weekend finals.
Advance ticket sales brought in just $310,000, far below the $1.12 million projected.
A curling village built around the event with restaurants, bars and arcades has resembled a ghost town, generating just 15 percent of expected revenue.
The ongoing world championships is not the only crisis with which the WCF is wrestling.

On Tuesday a group from Kamloops, British Columbia, stepped forward to host next year's world championships, saving the WCF the embarrassment of being unable to stage a championship just two months after their Olympic debut.
For almost two years the WCF had been trying to convince Glasgow to stage the event but the city refused claiming it was impossible to do so without sustaining a huge loss.

"There's no question that failing to stage a championship a few months after being in the Olympics would have tarnished the sport, maybe irreparably, in the eyes of the IOC," said Resby Couts, executive director of the 1995 world championships in Brandon, Manitoba, the last to realise a profit.
"The sport is guaranteed two Olympics but if it wants to stay a part of the Olympics it has to have a viable world championships and people watching in Japan."
Dave Parkes, president of the Canadian Curling Association, admitted Kamloops had been urged to take on the championships but did so only after negotiating major concessions from the WCF.
That, in turn, has forced the WCF to go cap in hand to the IOC and finance director Bob Whitehead acknowledges their assistance has averted disaster for now.

"We were advanced $400,000 by the IOC for the next two years to augment our cash flow, to help us stay alive and continue our programmes," said Whitehead. "This year and next would have been difficult without it."
